title: Quiz: binary arithmetic
prompt: Extended-precision carry chains, the shift-and-add multiplication algorithm, and the flag rules behind signed comparison.

questions.question: A 192-bit value is held in three 64-bit registers. Two such values are added low word first. Which instruction sequence is correct for the low, middle, and high words?
options: add, add, add
adc, adc, adc
adds, adds, adds
adds, adcs, adc
questions.explanation: The low word uses adds so its carry-out lands in the C flag. The middle word uses adcs to fold that carry in and set the next one. The high word uses adc, which consumes the last carry but does not need to produce one.
questions.hint: The first instruction has to create the carry, the middle one has to pass it along, and the last one only has to consume it.

questions.question: Which sequence is the subtraction counterpart of adds, adcs, adc for extended-precision arithmetic?
options: subs, sbcs, sbc
sub, sbc, sbc
subs, subs, sub
sub, sub, sub
questions.explanation: subs does the low-order subtraction and records the borrow in C, which the hardware clears when a borrow was needed. sbcs folds that borrow into the middle subtraction and updates C again, and sbc consumes the final borrow. Only the s-suffixed forms write the flags, so a plain sub cannot pass a borrow onward.
questions.hint: Same shape as the addition chain: set, propagate, consume.

questions.question: In the shift-and-add multiplication algorithm for M * N, when is the multiplicand M added to the accumulator T?
options: When the highest bit of the multiplier N is 1.
When the lowest bit of the multiplier, N[0], is 1.
On every iteration.
Only when the multiplier N is negative.
questions.explanation: Each iteration tests N[0], the low bit of the multiplier, and adds M to T only when that bit is 1. The iteration then shifts M left by one and N right by one, so the next bit of N lines up with the next power-of-two multiple of M.
questions.hint: The algorithm inspects the rightmost bit of N on every pass.

questions.question: Multiplying two 64-bit values can produce a result that does not fit in one register. How is the full product held?
options: It always overwrites the multiplicand register, and the high half is lost.
It is truncated to the width of the operands, and nothing can recover the upper bits.
It sets the V flag whenever the result exceeds 64 bits, and the rest goes to x16.
It can need 128 bits: mul gives the low half and umulh or smulh the high half.
questions.explanation: The product of two N-bit values needs up to 2N bits. mul writes only the low 64 bits, so the high 64 bits come from a separate umulh (unsigned) or smulh (signed) instruction. None of the multiply instructions set the flags.
questions.hint: Think about the widest result two 64-bit operands can produce, and how many registers that takes.

questions.question: Why can the signed lt condition not be decided by testing the Negative (N) flag alone?
options: N is never written by a subtraction, so the sign of a cmp result has to come from V alone.
The Zero flag always overrides N, so an equal pair would otherwise be reported as less.
Signed overflow can flip the result's sign bit, so V has to be checked too.
The Carry flag decides every signed comparison, and N only matters after an addition.
questions.explanation: cmp compares by subtracting, and when that subtraction overflows the sign bit of the result is the opposite of the true sign of the difference. lt is therefore defined as N != V, which stays correct in exactly the cases where N on its own would lie.
questions.hint: The course defines signed lt as N != V. Ask what V is telling you that N cannot.
